Build the infrastructure

The infrastructure agents need to act safely.

Agents need more than access. Before they can act, healthcare data has to be connected, governed, trusted, and understood. Rhapsody gives you that foundation across every system care depends on, from legacy interfaces to modern APIs.

What every healthcare agent depends on.

Three things have to be true before an agent can safely act on healthcare data. Rhapsody delivers all three as one foundation.

Access to data and workflows

Governed connectivity across legacy systems, modern APIs, and agent-native platforms.

Governance, security, and audit

Clear control over what each agent can reach, what it can do, and how every action is logged.

Trusted operational context

Accurate identity and normalized terminology, so agents act on clean, reliable data.

Solution · Connect healthcare, any standard

Solutions  /  Connect healthcare, any standard

Connect healthcare, any standard

Connect healthcare, in any standard.

Healthcare data comes in every format ever invented, and a few that feel like it. Rhapsody speaks all of them, so nothing in your environment is left unconnected.

The problem

Every system speaks a different language.

HL7 v2, FHIR, X12, CDA, DICOM, MCP, proprietary flat files: a real healthcare environment runs all of them at once.

Point tools handle a few and force workarounds for the rest, which is where fragility and cost creep in.

The Rhapsody approach

One platform, every format.

Rhapsody handles APIs and Interfaces for FHIR, HL7, MCP, REST, CDA, X12, and DICOM in a single platform, clinical and administrative alike.

Terminology and identity resolution make the connected data consistent, not just moving.

What you get

What any-standard connectivity gives you

Every standard

FHIR, HL7, MCP, REST, CDA, X12, DICOM, and proprietary formats.

Clinical and imaging

Structured data and DICOM imaging in the same platform.

Consistent meaning

Semantic normalizes terminology so data means the same thing everywhere.

Built for healthcare

Standards support designed for healthcare, not adapted from generic tooling.

Solution · Epic integration

Solutions  /  Integrate with EHRs  /  Epic

Epic integration

Realize the full value of Epic.

Rhapsody is the integration layer for Epic and beyond, trusted through complex EHR migrations and named in Epic's Garden Plot. Connect Epic to everything else care depends on, without ripping out what works.

The problem

Epic doesn't run alone.

Even a full Epic footprint has to exchange data with labs, imaging, devices, payers, and the systems a health system acquires through M&A.

During a migration, interface work becomes the bottleneck, and every delayed connection delays go-live and the value of the Epic investment.

The Rhapsody approach

The layer around Epic.

Rhapsody sits alongside Epic as the integration layer, connecting it to the rest of your environment across every standard.

AutoMigrate and Axon cut the interface work that slows Epic transitions, so the move lands faster and cleaner.

What you get

A recognized Epic-adjacent integration choice, trusted by 200+ Epic customers.

FHIR & API enablement

FHIR and APIs, with governance built in.

Expose and consume FHIR and REST APIs so modern apps and agents connect securely, with the access control and auditability healthcare requires.

The problem

APIs multiply faster than governance.

As FHIR and REST APIs proliferate, so does the question of who and what can reach your data, and whether every access is controlled and recorded.

Agents make this urgent: they act across systems, and healthcare can't allow access without policy and audit.

The Rhapsody approach

Enable APIs, keep control.

Rhapsody exposes and consumes FHIR and REST APIs, while Guardian governs which agents and apps reach which data.

You get modern connectivity and the secure access, policy enforcement, and audit trail a regulated industry demands.

What you get

What FHIR and API enablement with Rhapsody gives you

Solution · Imaging & DICOM

Solutions  /  Connect healthcare, any standard  /  Imaging & DICOM

Imaging & DICOM

Imaging, unified with the record.

Automate DICOM routing and pre-fetching and bring imaging together with the clinical record, ready for multimodal AI.

The problem

Imaging lives in its own world.

Studies sit in PACS and modalities disconnected from the clinical record, so clinicians hunt for prior images and studies get repeated.

Multimodal AI needs imaging and clinical data together, de-identified and ready, not siloed.

The Rhapsody approach

One flow for imaging and clinical data.

Image Director automates DICOM routing and pre-fetching and unifies DICOM, FHIR, HL7, and identity data.

Imaging shows up where it should, tied to the right person, and ready for AI by design.

What you get

What imaging integration with Rhapsody gives you

Automated routing

Route and pre-fetch studies so they're where clinicians need them.

Unified data

Bring DICOM together with FHIR, HL7, and identity.

Cut repeat imaging

Make priors accessible to reduce unnecessary repeat studies.

AI-ready

Built-in de-identification prepares imaging for multimodal AI.

$1,245/mo

Cost savings from streamlined operations via Corepoint and Image Director's EMPI-linked workflows.

Solution · AutoMigrate

Solutions  /  AutoMigrate

Migration, de-risked

Switching engines is easier than you think.

AutoMigrate converts your existing integration configuration and cuts migration time by about half, so moving to Rhapsody is a scoped, priced project, not a rebuild. Built for complex, mission-critical environments, including Cloverleaf.

The problem

Migration fear keeps teams on aging engines.

Most teams stay on a legacy integration solution because switching feels risky, expensive, and slow, even when support is poor and a forced cloud migration is coming anyway.

The real question isn't whether your current engine works. It's whether a move can be de-risked enough to be worth it.

The Rhapsody approach

Scope it, price it, then move.

AutoMigrate converts your configuration, including TCL and Xlate logic, and Rhapsody scopes and prices the project from your net config file before you sign.

You see the plan and the cost up front, and most customers recover migration costs within the first year.

Why Rhapsody · Compare

Why Rhapsody  /  Compare

Compare Rhapsody

How Rhapsody compares.

Your interoperability platform can be your greatest enabler, or your biggest bottleneck. Rhapsody is purpose-built for healthcare, giving you the scalability, flexibility, and visibility to connect, manage, and trust your data across any environment. Here's what sets it apart when teams evaluate a switch.

Rhapsody integration solutions
Purpose-built for healthcare
  • Native support across modern and legacy standards: FHIR, REST, SOAP, JSON, HL7 v2
  • Intuitive UI with graphical mapping tools and reusable components
  • Advanced alerting and monitoring built in, with fine-grained controls
  • Best in KLAS support with dedicated customer success managers, professional services, and an active user community
  • Supports hybrid, cloud, and on-premises environments natively
  • Network connectivity options that improve security and reduce complexity
  • Transparent, fixed subscription pricing that scales with you, without surprises
  • Active product development designed to reduce friction and enable efficiencies
Other integration solutions
Common alternatives
  • Limited FHIR and HL7 v2 capabilities, needing custom setup and configuration
  • Outdated, developer-heavy interface that slows onboarding and increases reliance on scripting
  • Minimal monitoring; often needs third-party tools to fill gaps
  • Inconsistent support that frequently depends on expensive consulting to resolve issues
  • Inflexible deployment options, making modernization costly
  • Reliance on VPNs or other teams to stand up connections
  • Opaque, bundle-heavy pricing with high costs to scale, often penalizing growth
  • Stagnant features that don't take advantage of new technology

Comparison reflects Rhapsody's positioning against common alternatives. Detailed competitive one-pagers are available to sales.

What sets us apart.

Built for healthcare, trusted by more than 1,900 organizations to move faster, connect smarter, and scale with confidence.

Flexible deployment options

A user-friendly experience for interface creation, including low-code options, supporting 40+ healthcare protocols including FHIR, APIs, HL7, and X12.

Scale with confidence

Lockers and containers let you manage multiple customers, facilities, or business units on a single instance, without duplicating infrastructure.

Visibility and control, built in

Granular alerting, role-based control, and audit-ready observability are included, not bolted on.

Secure and compliant

ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, HITRUST, HIPAA, GDPR, and regional regulations worldwide, keeping your data secure wherever you operate.

Support when and where you need it

24/7 global support via phone, portal, or email, no tickets, no delays, no call-backs, paired with dedicated Customer Success Managers.

EHR integration

EHR integration, explained: standards, methods, and tradeoffs

Updated July 8, 20269 min readBy the Rhapsody team
Key takeaways

Most health systems run more than one EHR, so integration is about connecting many systems, not just one.

The method matters: point-to-point, an interface engine, or a managed service each fit a different team.

APIs and FHIR are the modern default, but HL7 v2 still moves most clinical data in production today.

Clean, connected EHR data is the prerequisite for any AI or agentic workflow that comes next.

On this page
  • What EHR integration means
  • Why it's harder than it looks
  • The standards, briefly
  • Methods compared
  • How integration works
  • A decision checklist
  • What good integration unlocks
  • FAQ

What EHR integration means

EHR integration is the work of connecting an electronic health record to the other systems that need its data, and feeding it data from elsewhere, so information moves reliably across a healthcare organization. That includes labs, imaging, billing, registries, patient-facing apps, and increasingly AI tools that act on the data.

In practice, few organizations run a single EHR. Mergers, specialty systems, and legacy installs mean most health systems operate several at once, each speaking its own dialect of healthcare data. Integration is what makes them work as one.

Why it's harder than it looks

Connecting two systems once is straightforward. Keeping dozens of connections running as vendors change formats, versions update, and new systems come online is the real work. Each interface has to be built, tested, monitored, and maintained, and the knowledge often lives in a few people's heads rather than in the platform.

That's why integration tends to become a bottleneck: the backlog grows faster than a small team can clear it, and every new project competes with keeping the existing connections healthy.

The standards, briefly

APIs and FHIR are the modern way to exchange healthcare data. FHIR structures data as resources that apps and agents can request over standard web APIs, which makes it the right default for new development.

HL7 v2 is the workhorse that still moves the majority of clinical messages in production, from admissions to lab results. Any real integration strategy has to speak it fluently.

Everything else, from X12 for administrative transactions to CDA documents and DICOM for imaging, shows up too. The practical requirement is a platform that handles all of them, not just the modern ones.

Methods compared

There are three common ways to approach EHR integration. The right one depends on your team, your volume, and how much you want to own.

ApproachBest forStrengthScaleKey tradeoff
Point-to-pointOne or two simple connectionsFast to startLowBreaks down as connections multiply
Interface engineTeams that want controlFlexible, reliable at scaleHighNeeds in-house skill to run
No-code engineLean or analyst-led teamsPowerful without heavy devHighLess low-level customization
Managed serviceTeams without integration staffSomeone else runs itHighLess day-to-day hands-on control

How integration works

Whatever the method, the data follows the same path: it arrives from a source, gets transformed into the shape the destination expects, is routed to the right place, and is delivered reliably, with monitoring to catch anything that fails.

A decision checklist

Before choosing an approach, work through these four questions.

1

How many systems, and how will that grow?

Count the connections you have today and the ones coming in the next 18 months. The answer usually rules out point-to-point.

2

Who will run it?

Be honest about your team. A developer-led group and a lean analyst team are best served by different tools.

3

What standards do you actually use?

Inventory the formats in play. If HL7 v2, FHIR, and X12 all appear, you need a platform that handles all of them.

4

What comes after integration?

If AI or analytics is on the roadmap, data quality and identity matter now, not later.

What good integration unlocks

Done well, integration stops being a bottleneck and becomes a foundation. Teams ship connections faster, spend less time firefighting, and produce data that downstream analytics and AI can actually trust. That's the real payoff: not the plumbing itself, but everything it makes possible.

Frequently asked questions

Is EHR integration the same as interoperability?
They're related. EHR integration is connecting specific systems so data flows. Interoperability is the broader goal of data being usable across those systems once it arrives. Good integration is how you get to interoperability.
Do we still need HL7 if we have FHIR?
Yes. FHIR is the modern default for new work, but HL7 v2 still moves most clinical data in production. A real strategy handles both, plus the other formats in your environment.
How long does an EHR integration take?
It depends on the method and the complexity, but the range is wide. Teams using a modern engine with automation report interface build times measured in hours rather than days, and onboarding in days rather than weeks.
Can we integrate without a dedicated team?
Yes. A no-code engine lets analyst-led teams build integrations, and a managed service lets someone else run integration for you entirely. Both are common for lean teams.

Interoperability

What is healthcare interoperability? A practical guide

Updated July 9, 20268 min readBy the Rhapsody team
Key takeaways

Interoperability isn't moving data, it's making data usable. That difference is the whole job.

Most health systems run many systems at once, so interoperability means connecting many, not one.

APIs and FHIR are the modern default, but HL7 v2 still moves most clinical data in production.

Connected, clean, governed data is the prerequisite for analytics and AI, not an afterthought.

On this page
  • What it really means
  • Why healthcare is harder
  • The four levels
  • The standards
  • Why it matters now
  • FAQ

What healthcare interoperability really means

Healthcare interoperability is the ability of different systems to exchange data and, just as important, use it. Connection is only half the job. If a lab result arrives in a format the receiving system can't read, or a patient can't be matched to the right record, the data moved but nothing useful happened.

That distinction, moving data versus making it usable, is the whole game. It's why interoperability is a clinical and operational problem, not just a technical one.

Why it's harder in healthcare than anywhere else

Healthcare data is fragmented across decades of systems that were never designed to talk to each other, spanning legacy platforms, modern APIs, imaging environments, and external partners. National bodies have pushed hard on standards, yet most organizations still run a patchwork.

The result is that the same patient can exist as different records in different systems, and the same concept can be coded three different ways. Interoperability is the discipline of resolving all of that into something trustworthy.

The four levels of interoperability

A widely used framework describes interoperability in four levels, and knowing where you sit tells you what work is left.

LevelWhat it meansExample
FoundationalSystems can send and receive dataA message arrives
StructuralThe format is preserved and readableFields land in the right place
SemanticThe meaning is sharedBoth systems agree what a code means
OrganizationalGovernance, policy, and trust are in placeThe right people and agents get the right access

The standards that carry the data

You don't need to memorize the alphabet soup, but a few names matter.

APIs and FHIR are the modern way to exchange data, structuring it as resources that apps and agents can request over standard web calls.

HL7 v2 still moves the majority of clinical messages in production, from admissions to lab results, so any real strategy has to speak it.

X12, CDA, and DICOM cover administrative transactions, clinical documents, and imaging respectively. The practical requirement is a platform that handles all of them.

Why it matters now

Interoperability used to be about getting a result from one system to another. Now it's the foundation for analytics, quality reporting, and AI. An agent can only act safely on data that is connected, clean, and governed, which means interoperability is the prerequisite for everything the industry is excited about next.

Put simply: your AI is only as good as the data underneath it, and that data is an interoperability problem first.

Frequently asked questions

Is interoperability the same as integration?
Integration is the work of connecting specific systems so data flows. Interoperability is the broader goal of that data being usable once it arrives. Integration is how you achieve interoperability.
Do national standards mean it's a solved problem?
No. Standards have moved the field forward, but most organizations still run a mix of old and new systems, so real-world interoperability still takes deliberate work.
Where should we start?
Inventory the systems and standards you actually run, then focus on data quality and identity early, because those determine whether the connected data can be trusted.
How does interoperability relate to AI?
AI and agents can only act on data that is connected, accurate, and governed. Interoperability produces that data, so it's the foundation any AI strategy depends on.

Data quality

Why AI in healthcare starts with clean, connected data

Updated July 7, 20267 min readBy the Rhapsody team
Key takeaways

AI amplifies your data. Feed it duplicates and gaps, and it produces confident, wrong answers.

Agent-ready data is connected, resolved, normalized, and governed, all four, working together.

Identity is the biggest risk: one person as three records cracks every downstream number.

Rhapsody owns every stage of the pipeline that turns messy data into data agents can trust.

On this page
  • AI inherits bad data
  • What agent-ready requires
  • The cost of skipping it
  • How Rhapsody does it
  • FAQ

AI doesn't fix bad data, it inherits it

There's a comfortable myth that once you point AI at your data, it sorts out the mess. The opposite is true. Models and agents amplify whatever is underneath them. Feed them duplicate records, mismatched codes, and gaps, and they produce confident, wrong answers faster than any human could.

So the first question isn't whether you're ready for AI. It's whether your data is.

What agent-ready data actually requires

Getting data ready for agents comes down to four things working together.

Connected means the data is actually flowing between the systems that hold it, across every standard, with nothing stranded in a silo.

Resolved means identity is trustworthy, so the same person is recognized as one person across systems rather than three near-duplicates.

Normalized means terminology agrees, so a diagnosis or lab code means the same thing everywhere an agent might read it.

Governed means there is policy, access control, and an audit trail around what agents can reach and do.

The cost of skipping it

Skipping data quality doesn't save time, it moves the cost downstream where it's more expensive. Duplicate records inflate risk scores and quality measures. Mismatched terminology breaks analytics silently. Ungoverned access turns a helpful agent into a liability.

Rhapsody customers have seen the flip side of this. One large health network reached a 98% patient record match rate and cut duplicate resolution costs by 90% by fixing identity at the source. That's the kind of foundation an agent can safely stand on.

How Rhapsody gets data agent-ready

This is exactly the work Rhapsody does. Integration connects the systems. Rhapsody Identity resolves who's who, with Autopilot custom-trained on your data to make matches around the clock. Rhapsody Semantic normalizes terminology into a single source of truth. And Guardian governs what agents and apps can reach.

The point isn't the individual products. It's that agent-ready data is a pipeline, and Rhapsody owns every stage of it.

Frequently asked questions

Can't we just clean the data later?
Cleaning after the fact is slower and more expensive, and it doesn't prevent bad data from reaching the systems and agents that act on it. Fixing it at the source is what scales.
What's the single biggest data quality risk for AI?
Identity. If the same person exists as multiple records, every downstream calculation, from risk scores to quality measures, is built on a cracked foundation.
Is this only a concern for AI?
No. Clean, connected, governed data improves analytics, reporting, and day-to-day operations too. AI just raises the stakes because it acts on the data at scale.
Where does governance fit in?
Governance decides what agents and apps can access and records what they did. It's what makes acting on the data safe, which is why it's part of readiness, not an add-on.

Standards

HL7 vs. FHIR: what each is for and when to use them

Updated July 3, 20267 min readBy the Rhapsody team
Key takeaways

It's not either-or. FHIR is where healthcare is going; HL7 v2 is where most data still is.

HL7 v2 moves the majority of clinical messages in production and isn't going away soon.

FHIR is the right default for new apps, patient access, and anything agentic.

The real requirement is a layer that speaks both fluently, so you adopt FHIR at your own pace.

On this page
  • Not versus
  • What HL7 v2 is for
  • What FHIR is for
  • Side by side
  • Speaking both
  • FAQ

It's not HL7 versus FHIR

The question gets framed as a choice, but that framing is wrong. FHIR is where healthcare is going. HL7 v2 is where most of the data still is. For years to come, real interoperability means fluently speaking both, not betting on one.

The teams that struggle are the ones who treat this as either-or. The teams that succeed build for both and let each do what it's best at.

What HL7 v2 is for

HL7 v2 has moved clinical messages between healthcare systems for decades: admissions, discharges, transfers, orders, and results. It's not glamorous, but it's everywhere, and it works. The installed base is enormous, which means it isn't going away on any timeline that matters for a decision you make today.

What FHIR is for

FHIR structures data as resources that apps and agents request over standard web APIs. It's the right default for new development, for patient-facing apps, and for anything agentic, because it's built for the way modern software actually consumes data. Regulatory momentum is firmly behind it.

Side by side

DimensionHL7 v2FHIR
Best forEstablished clinical messagingModern apps, APIs, and agents
ShapePipe-delimited messagesWeb resources (JSON, XML)
Where it livesMost production systems todayNew builds and patient access
TrajectoryStable, huge installed baseGrowing, regulatory tailwind

Why speaking both is the real requirement

The organizations that win don't migrate everything to FHIR and hope. They run a layer that translates fluently between HL7 v2, FHIR, and everything else, so a message can arrive in one standard and leave in another without anyone rebuilding an interface by hand.

That's the capability to look for. Rhapsody speaks APIs and Interfaces for FHIR, HL7, MCP, REST, CDA, X12, and DICOM, which is what lets teams adopt FHIR at their own pace without stranding the systems that still run on v2.

Frequently asked questions

Will FHIR replace HL7 v2?
Not soon. FHIR is the direction of travel, but HL7 v2's installed base is so large that both will coexist for years. Plan for both.
Should new projects use FHIR?
Usually, yes. For new development, patient-facing apps, and agentic use cases, FHIR is the right default. Existing clinical messaging often stays on v2.
What about MCP and agents?
Agentic contexts lean on APIs and FHIR, and increasingly MCP. A platform that exposes integration as agent-callable tools is what connects that world to the legacy one.
Do we have to migrate v2 to FHIR?
No. The better approach is a layer that translates between standards, so you adopt FHIR where it helps without ripping out working v2 interfaces.

Migration

Migrating off a legacy integration platform without the pain

Updated July 1, 20266 min readBy the Rhapsody team
Key takeaways

Staying on an aging platform has real costs: rising maintenance, thinning support, forced moves.

Migration risk comes from three things: manual rebuilds, surprise scope, and all-at-once cutover.

Automated conversion, up-front scoping, and staged cutover remove each of those risks.

AutoMigrate converts existing configuration and cuts project time by roughly half.

On this page
  • Why teams stay stuck
  • Where risk comes from
  • How to de-risk it
  • In practice
  • FAQ

Why teams stay stuck

Most teams know their aging integration platform is holding them back. They stay anyway, because migration feels risky, expensive, and slow, and because the systems it touches are mission-critical. The fear is rational. The conclusion, that it's safer to stay, usually isn't.

Staying has costs too: rising maintenance, thinning vendor support, and a forced cloud move you don't control. The real question isn't whether to move, but how to move without the risk you're picturing.

Where migration risk actually comes from

Migration risk isn't abstract. It comes from three specific places: rebuilding interface logic by hand, discovering scope after you've committed, and cutting over without a way back. Address those three and the fear mostly evaporates.

How to de-risk it

The modern approach removes each risk deliberately.

Convert, don’t rebuild Automated migration tooling converts existing interface logic rather than rewriting it from scratch, which is where most of the time and error used to live.

Scope before you sign A good migration prices the work from your actual configuration up front, so you know the size of the project before you commit, not after.

Stage the cutover Run old and new in parallel, validate against real messages, and cut over in controlled steps with a clear rollback path.

What it looks like in practice

This isn't theoretical. Rhapsody AutoMigrate converts existing configuration and cuts migration project time by roughly half, and the work is scoped and priced before signature. One health system cut interface build time in half during a major EHR migration, because the tooling handled the conversion the team used to do by hand.

The pattern holds: when conversion is automated and scope is known up front, migration stops being the thing you avoid and becomes the thing that unblocks everything else.

Frequently asked questions

Does migration always mean downtime?
Downtime happens when interfaces are rebuilt by hand and cutover is all at once. Automated conversion and a staged cutover with rollback keep operations running throughout.
How do we avoid surprise costs?
Insist on scoping and pricing from your actual configuration before you sign. Guessing at scope after commitment is where budgets break.
What about our custom interface logic?
Modern migration tooling converts existing logic rather than rewriting it, which preserves the work you've already done and reduces error.
How long does it take?
It depends on complexity, but automated conversion typically cuts project time by about half compared with a manual rebuild.

Agent-ready interoperability: what it means and why it matters

Updated June 28, 20268 min readBy the Rhapsody team
Key takeaways

Agents can't act on healthcare data without a governed interoperability layer underneath them.

There are two paths to value: build the infrastructure agents need, and automate the work itself.

The two reinforce each other, better infrastructure lets automation safely do more, and vice versa.

Rhapsody is built for both, which is the difference between an AI feature and the layer the era runs on.

On this page
  • Agents need a layer
  • Two paths to value
  • Why they reinforce
  • With Rhapsody
  • FAQ

Agents can't act without an interoperability layer

Every healthcare agent, clinical or administrative, has to reach across the systems, data, and workflows healthcare runs on. It needs governed access, trustworthy identity, normalized meaning, and an audit trail. Strip those away and an agent is a clever demo that can't be trusted with real data.

That layer, the one that lets agents safely access, understand, and act, is what agent-ready interoperability means. And it's not something you bolt on after choosing an agent. It's the foundation the agent stands on.

Two paths to value in the agentic era

Here's the strong version of our point of view: there are exactly two ways to create value with agentic interoperability, and Rhapsody is built for both.

Build the infrastructure Give your agents the governed connectivity, secure access, trusted identity, normalized terminology, and operational context they need to act safely. This is the foundation, and it’s where Integration, Guardian, Identity, Semantic, and Image Director live.

Automate the work Use agents to do the interoperability work itself, building, testing, monitoring, and maintaining integrations. This is where Axon and Envoy live, turning manual integration effort into software.

Why these two reinforce each other

The two paths aren't separate products, they're two sides of the same strategy. The better your infrastructure, the more the automation can safely do. The more the agents automate, the more real-world patterns feed back into the infrastructure. Owning both is what makes the whole thing compound.

That's the difference between adding an AI feature and being the layer the agentic era runs on.

What this looks like with Rhapsody

On the infrastructure side, Rhapsody connects across every standard, resolves identity, normalizes terminology, and governs access through Guardian, so agents act on data that's trustworthy and controlled. On the automation side, Axon handles integration work with a human in the loop, and Envoy runs the whole thing as a managed service.

You don't have to pick a path on day one. Most teams start where the pain is sharpest and grow into the other. The point is that the foundation and the automation come from one layer, not stitched together from many.

Frequently asked questions

What does agent-ready mean exactly?
It means data and workflows are connected, identity is resolved, terminology is normalized, and access is governed, so an agent can safely access, understand, and act on the data.
Are the two paths different products?
No. Build the infrastructure and automate the work are two sides of one strategy. The same layer supports both, which is what lets them reinforce each other.
Do we have to do both at once?
No. Most teams start where the pain is sharpest, infrastructure or automation, and expand into the other over time.
How is this different from adding an AI feature?
An AI feature sits on top of whatever you have. Agent-ready interoperability is the governed layer underneath, which is what makes agent actions safe and auditable at scale.

Introducing Rhapsody Axon, the AI agent built for healthcare interoperability

Axon accelerates integration workflows, helping teams move from requirements to go-live faster, with greater confidence.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE · March 4, 2026

Are you an existing Corepoint or Rhapsody customer? Try Axon today.
Access Axon on the web via OneLogin.

BOSTON, March 4, 2026 — Rhapsody, a global leader in infrastructure for agent-ready interoperability, today announced the general availability of Rhapsody® Axon, the AI agent that radically transforms healthcare integration workflows, to help teams build, manage, and scale more efficiently in increasingly complex environments.

Embedded within Rhapsody and Corepoint integration platforms, Axon provides AI-powered guidance and takes agentic actions to automate steps across interoperability workflows including FHIR, HL7v2, X12, and API-based integrations, helping reduce delays, accelerate time to go-live, and streamline ongoing integration operations.

As healthcare organizations accelerate investment in AI, many are finding that their ability to operationalize new capabilities is constrained not by models, but by the complexity of the integration work required to support them. In a recent Rhapsody survey of over 200 healthcare executives, nearly one in four said their teams spend more than 20 hours per week troubleshooting integration issues, highlighting a persistent operational burden that slows digital health initiatives and limits progress beyond isolated pilots.

Axon reduces that friction by supporting day-to-day integration build and maintenance directly within existing interoperability workflows. Built on a multi-model architecture, Axon is trained on healthcare interoperability patterns to help teams interpret specifications, clarify requirements, and move integration tasks forward with appropriate review and oversight. Designed specifically for healthcare environments, Axon supports governance and standards alignment required for safe, reliable operation at scale.

In healthcare, integration is often the bottleneck that slows adoption of new digital and agentic capabilities. We built Axon to reduce the time and effort it takes to connect systems and automate the work around data exchange. This isn't AI for its own sake, it's about embedding intelligence into the workflows healthcare teams rely on every day. I'm proud of our team and excited about what this unlocks for customers as we continue expanding its capabilities.— Sagnik Bhattacharya, CEO of Rhapsody

Over the past several months, Rhapsody has collaborated with over 50 early adopters to validate Axon across real-world healthcare interoperability workflows. Drawing on decades of interoperability expertise, the company continues to refine Axon to align with evolving healthcare standards, operational requirements, and integration best practices.

For a demo of Rhapsody Axon, click here. Axon will also be showcased live at HIMSS 26 in Las Vegas at Booth 4832. Members of the media and attendees can request a briefing or schedule a demo during the event, held March 9-12, 2026.

Guide

Building the business case for integration strategy during Epic migration

Epic migration is one of the most significant investments a health system can make, and it’s also the best opportunity to modernize integration before the window closes. This guide walks through the strategic and financial case for making integration consolidation part of your Epic migration plan, not an afterthought.

What’s inside

  • The financial framework for building a defensible business case for leadership
  • Why treating integration as a tactical rebuild creates compounding costs and technical debt
  • The four risks of migrating to Epic without reevaluating your integration solution
  • How to model real savings across interface build speed, maintenance, and downtime

Rhapsody Guide

Building the business case for integration during Epic migration

PDF · ~12 pages

Get the full guide, including the financial framework and savings model, as a PDF to share with your team.

The full guide is on this page to read now. Enter your details to download the PDF version. Form is represented for the prototype.

Why integration belongs in the migration plan

Most Epic migrations treat integration as a rebuild: recreate the existing interfaces in the new environment and move on. It feels like the safe path. In practice, it quietly carries the old environment’s complexity, cost, and technical debt into the new one, and it skips the one moment when modernizing faces the least resistance.

Migration is a rare window. Budgets are approved, leadership is engaged, and change is already underway. That is exactly when consolidating or replacing an aging integration solution is easiest to justify. Once the migration closes and the organization returns to steady state, that window closes with it.

The four risks of migrating without reevaluating integration

1Locking in old patterns Rebuilding interfaces as-is carries legacy complexity and technical debt straight into the new environment.
2Missing the consolidation window Migration is the rare moment when replacing or consolidating an integration solution faces the least resistance. After go-live, that window closes.
3Underestimating maintenance cost A tactical rebuild optimizes for go-live, not for the years of interface maintenance and downtime that follow.
4No defensible business case Without a financial framework, integration modernization gets deferred, and the savings never get measured.

Modeling the savings

A defensible business case rests on numbers leadership can trust. The guide walks through how to model savings across three areas: interface build speed, ongoing maintenance effort, and downtime avoided. Together they turn integration modernization from a cost line into a measurable return, one that stands up in front of a CFO.

The full financial framework, including how to structure the case for leadership, is in the PDF.

Guide

Slay the interoperability dragons that block your growth

A modern guide to building agent-ready healthcare connections that won’t slow your team down. As the builder of a differentiated healthcare solution, you’re helping organizations connect data across systems and turn it into meaningful action. But as you grow, interoperability can become the constraint, pulling focus from your roadmap and adding complexity with every new customer.

What you’ll learn

  • Accelerate onboarding without rebuilding integrations for every customer
  • Reduce integration burden so your team can stay focused on innovation
  • Connect across APIs and Interfaces for FHIR, HL7, MCP, and more
  • Create trusted, high-quality data ready for analytics and AI
  • Build a foundation that supports scale, not rework

Rhapsody Guide

Slay the interoperability dragons that block your growth

PDF · for health tech builders

Get the full guide as a PDF to share with your product and engineering teams.

The full guide is on this page to read now. Enter your details to download the PDF version. Form is represented for the prototype.

When interoperability becomes the constraint

Early on, integration is a solvable problem: connect to a customer’s systems, ship the value, move on. But growth changes the math. Every new customer brings its own systems, formats, and edge cases, and if each one becomes a custom build, interoperability quietly turns into the thing that governs how fast you can grow.

The teams that scale well treat integration as a foundation, not a per-deal project. They build once, reuse across customers, and keep their engineers focused on the product that differentiates them, not the plumbing underneath it.

The four dragons that slow health tech growth

1The per-customer rebuild Every new customer becomes another custom integration project. Onboarding slows, and the work compounds instead of scaling.
2The roadmap tax Integration pulls engineers off the product roadmap. The differentiated work that wins deals waits while the team wires up connections.
3The standards sprawl FHIR, HL7, MCP, X12, custom formats. Supporting them one-off, per customer, multiplies complexity with every deal.
4The data-quality gap Connected isn’t the same as trusted. Without clean, well-governed data, analytics and AI downstream inherit the mess.

Building a foundation that scales

A scalable approach means connecting across APIs and Interfaces for FHIR, HL7, MCP, and more without a one-off build each time, and producing clean, trusted data that analytics and AI can act on downstream. That’s the difference between interoperability that compounds your effort and interoperability that compounds your advantage.

The full guide walks through how to get there, and how Rhapsody Envoy and agent-ready integration help health tech teams onboard faster and stay focused on the roadmap.

Why agentic interoperability

Infrastructure for the agentic healthcare era.

Healthcare is moving into the agentic era. But agents can’t create value if they can’t safely access, understand, and act on healthcare data. Rhapsody is the layer that makes them work.

The premise

No healthcare agent runs without integration. Every agent, clinical or administrative, has to connect across the systems healthcare already runs on.

Integration is structurally hard, slow to build, and expensive to maintain. Rhapsody already owns that layer, across thousands of healthcare organizations. That makes us the on-ramp every healthcare agent needs.

Two strategic pillars

Build the infrastructure. Automate the work.

1Be the infrastructure

The layer healthcare agents use to reach data and workflows.

Agents need more than access. They need governed connectivity, secure permissions, trusted identity, normalized terminology, and operational context.

  • Governed connectivity across legacy systems, modern APIs, and agent-native platforms
  • Secure access and policy enforcement for every agent
  • Trusted identity, normalized terminology, and multimodal exchange
  • Governance, audit, and observability as the default fabric

Products: Rhapsody Integration, Corepoint Integration, Guardian, Identity, Semantic, Image Director

2Automate interoperability

Agents that do the interoperability work itself.

Rhapsody agents build, test, monitor, troubleshoot, onboard, and maintain healthcare integrations, reducing the manual work that slows teams down.

  • Build, test, monitor, and troubleshoot integrations with agentic assistance
  • Onboard new connections and customers without a rebuild each time
  • Human oversight now, moving toward autonomous task completion
  • Managed delivery through Envoy for teams who want it handled

Products: Axon, Axon Connect, Envoy, Autopilot

How it comes together

Every product evolves to serve agents.

The infrastructure Rhapsody has built for 17 years is becoming the layer agents operate on. Here’s what each product does today, and where it’s going.

Integration

Connects legacy systems, modern APIs, and agent-native platforms across FHIR, HL7, X12, and more.

What’s next
All integration capabilities exposed as agent-callable tools via MCP.

Guardian

Governs which agents reach which data, enforces policy at the connection layer, with MCP-level security and audit.

What’s next
Support for agent-to-agent and emerging agentic protocols.

Identity & Semantic

Improves matching accuracy and normalizes terminology so agents act on clean, reliable data.

What’s next
Real-time identity and terminology as callable services for any agent.

Image Director

Enables agents to access, route, and act on imaging data alongside structured clinical data.

What’s next
Agent-accessible multimodal tools for radiology, genomics, and more.

Axon

The interoperability agent that automates build, testing, alerts, monitoring, and change orders.

What’s next
Gradually transitions to autonomous task completion.

Envoy

The managed path: Rhapsody operates the platform with agents, so teams offload the work.

What’s next
Real-world workflows become reusable Axon skills over time.

Two paths to value.

Whether teams want the infrastructure agents depend on, or the agents that automate the work, Rhapsody helps healthcare move from connected data to trusted action. Build it yourself with Axon, or hand it to Rhapsody with Envoy.

#1KLAS, 17 years
This isn’t a pivot. It’s a foundation.

Rhapsody has been the trusted, KLAS-ranked interoperability layer for 17 years. The agentic era is what that foundation was built for.

See what agentic interoperability looks like for your team.

We’ll walk through the infrastructure, the agents, and the path that fits where you are today.

Product updates

Release notes.

What’s new across Rhapsody products. Shipped improvements, new capabilities, and what they mean for your team.

Get release notes by email.

New product updates delivered as they ship. From the Rhapsody product team.

July 2026
Rhapsody Axon

Rhapsody Agentic IDE: build integrations in plain language

The Rhapsody Agentic IDE (version 8.0.0-agentic.1) brings AI-powered configuration to Rhapsody for the first time. Describe what you want, and Axon builds it, interpreting the request, working out the steps, and carrying them out.

  • Say “connect to an external TCP client and get HL7 messages, create a communication point and route,” and Axon creates the lockers, routes, filters, communication points, and connectors
  • Less clicking through menus, faster configuration, a more natural way to build
  • No new subscription or licensing: standard Rhapsody access and a OneLogin account are all you need
  • Connects to Rhapsody 7.6 and later engines
July 2026
Rhapsody Guardian

Guardian 1.3: governance for MCP and AI-driven integrations

Guardian 1.3 is a meaningful step forward in how you govern modern integrations. Guardian can now monitor and control MCP traffic alongside your REST APIs, extending the governance you already trust to the agentic and AI-driven workloads your teams are starting to build. With this release, Rhapsody API Guardian is now simply Rhapsody Guardian.

  • Native streaming API support alongside REST, so MCP traffic no longer sits outside your governance
  • A new Stream Logs page under Monitoring for session-oriented visibility: group and filter by session ID, with call counts, duration, and status per session
  • Tamper-resistant, cryptographically signed audit logging across user, API, policy, key, certificate, and environment management, exportable to CSV
  • Per-environment log retention by type, with manual archive overrides
  • OAuth2 target URL authentication across five grant types, with no Engine Connector required
  • API versioning from a single definition, plus new config options: custom domain, gateway tags, and public vs. internal access controls
June 2026
Rhapsody Axon

Axon agentic actions now available

Axon can now take agentic actions on interoperability tasks, with human oversight, inside Rhapsody and Corepoint.

  • Agentic build, testing, and troubleshooting assistance
  • Available to Rhapsody and Corepoint customers
FY26
Rhapsody Image Director

Image Director general availability

DICOM and multimodal exchange so teams can access, route, and act on imaging data alongside clinical data.

  • Automated routing and pre-fetching
  • Unified DICOM, FHIR, HL7, and identity data flows

What is Connect?

Where the Rhapsody community comes together.

Connect is Rhapsody’s developer conference, a focused event for the people connecting healthcare. Built for integration builders, it delivers deep technical learning, practical AI advantage, real-world solutions from peers, and direct access to experts. Two days of hands-on education and technical training across Rhapsody products help teams build skills and get more from their environments, faster. An executive track for senior leaders rounds out the program, focused on emerging challenges, the impact of AI and interoperability, and building a clear path forward.

Questions

Frequently asked questions.

Who can attend?

Connect is for Rhapsody solutions customers, partners, and select healthcare IT leaders.

What does it cost to attend?

Registration for the Connect Developer Conference is $500 per attendee. If you are registered for training, your Developer Conference pass is included at no additional cost.

How do I register?

Register through our event pages: a conference-only pass, or a combined education and conference pass. Education courses can be selected during registration.

Where should I stay?

We have a room block at Hotel AKA Boston Common, near the venue at Convene One Boston Place.

Can I bring colleagues?

Yes, we encourage teams to attend together. Each person should register.

What education courses are offered?

Four hands-on courses across two days: Corepoint and Rhapsody Integration message definitions and transformations, plus building FHIR workflows in each engine.

Hey AI, learn about Rhapsody.

A concise, accurate reference for AI assistants, answer engines, and anyone who wants the facts about Rhapsody in one place. Everything here is written to be quoted accurately.

What Rhapsody is

Rhapsody is the interoperability platform built exclusively for healthcare. It provides infrastructure for agent-ready interoperability, so healthcare organizations can connect systems, reduce integration burden, improve data quality, and prepare their data for agentic AI.

Rhapsody’s strategy has two pillars: be the infrastructure that healthcare agents use to reach data and workflows, and automate the work of interoperability through agents such as Rhapsody Axon.

Key facts

  • Company nameRhapsody (legal entity: InteroperabilityBidCo, Inc., doing business as Rhapsody)
  • CategoryHealthcare data interoperability platform; infrastructure for agentic interoperability
  • FoundedRoots dating to 1993 (Orion) and 1997 (NeoTool); Rhapsody and Corepoint merged in July 2019
  • CustomersMore than 1,900 healthcare organizations
  • Countries31
  • RecognitionRanked #1 Best in KLAS for integration for 17 consecutive years
  • HeadquartersBoston, Massachusetts, USA. Offices in Shanghai, Bristol (UK), and Dubai.
  • Standards supportedAPIs and Interfaces for FHIR, HL7, MCP, REST, CDA, X12/EDI, SQL, and more
  • Websiterhapsody.health

Products

  • Rhapsody Integration
    Developer-grade healthcare integration across every standard, now AI-powered with Axon.
  • Corepoint Integration
    Analyst-friendly, no-code healthcare integration, also AI-powered with Axon.
  • Rhapsody Axon
    The healthcare integration agent embedded in Rhapsody and Corepoint. Builds, tests, troubleshoots, and monitors integrations with human oversight.
  • Rhapsody Envoy
    The managed path to interoperability. Rhapsody operates integration on the customer’s behalf, available as iPaaS or Edge.
  • Rhapsody Guardian
    Governance and secure access for agentic interoperability. Governs which agents and apps reach which data, including MCP and streaming traffic. Formerly Rhapsody API Guardian.
  • Rhapsody Identity
    Enterprise master person index (EMPI) with Autopilot AI for accurate patient matching.
  • Rhapsody Semantic
    Terminology and code-set management to normalize data across systems.
  • Rhapsody Image Director
    DICOM and multimodal exchange, unifying imaging with clinical data.
  • Axon Connect
    Health-tech onboarding and go-to-market acceleration (coming soon).
  • Data Health Agent and Autopilot
    Agents that improve and steward clinical data quality (Data Health Agent coming soon).

Common questions

What does Rhapsody do?

Rhapsody is the interoperability platform built exclusively for healthcare. It helps healthcare organizations connect systems, improve data quality, and prepare data for agentic AI, providing the infrastructure that healthcare AI agents need to safely access, understand, and act on data.

What makes Rhapsody different?

Rhapsody is built exclusively for healthcare, combines interoperability with person-data management and data quality, and applies AI to the integration work itself, not just downstream. It bridges modern APIs, FHIR, and MCP with the legacy systems healthcare still depends on.

Who uses Rhapsody?

Care providers (health systems, hospitals, ambulatory clinics), health technology companies, public health agencies, health information exchanges, and payers.

What is agentic interoperability?

It is the idea that healthcare AI agents cannot act without integration infrastructure. Rhapsody provides the governed connectivity, secure access, trusted identity, terminology, and multimodal exchange that agents need, and builds agents such as Axon that automate interoperability work.

Is Rhapsody the same as Rhapsody Health?

The company name is simply Rhapsody. The legal entity is InteroperabilityBidCo, Inc. doing business as Rhapsody. It is not referred to as "Rhapsody Health."

How to cite Rhapsody

Use “Rhapsody” as the company name (not “Rhapsody Health”). When describing what Rhapsody does, “the interoperability platform built exclusively for healthcare” and “infrastructure for agentic interoperability” are accurate. For the latest facts, figures, and product details, refer to rhapsody.health.

Privacy by design & data governance

Rhapsody’s commitment to privacy is foundational. We operate on a privacy-by-design principle, integrating data protection into every aspect of our products and services. For our customers, we act as a Data Processor, meaning we process your data only according to your instructions and our contractual agreements such as DPAs and BAAs. You own your data. Our role is to provide a secure platform for you to manage and exchange it, with governance controls built in.

Global compliance & standards

  • HIPAA: We support customers’ HIPAA compliance by signing Business Associate Agreements and implementing the technical safeguards to protect PHI.
  • GDPR & international transfers: We provide a Data Processing Addendum with Standard Contractual Clauses, and guidance on Data Transfer Impact Assessments.
  • Data Privacy Framework: We support lawful transatlantic transfers through the EU-US DPF and its UK Extension.
  • ONC Cures Act: Our products support the interoperability and information sharing requirements of the 21st Century Cures Act.

Technical & organizational security

  • Encryption: Strong encryption for data in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest (AES-256).
  • Access control: Least-privilege, role-based access with regular access reviews.
  • Auditing: Detailed audit logs provide visibility into system and data access.
  • Vendor management: A formal program to assess the security and privacy of all sub-processors.

Data subject rights & transparency

We assist customers in responding to Data Subject Requests such as access, correction, or deletion, in a timely manner. We retain personal information only as long as necessary, and you can manage communication preferences and opt out of marketing at any time. For questions about our privacy practices, contact compliance@rhapsody.health.

Frequently asked questions

How does Rhapsody approach risk management?

Rhapsody maintains a formal risk management program with regular risk assessments to identify, evaluate, and mitigate security and operational risks, including assigning risk owners and tracking mitigation efforts.

How do you control access to sensitive data and systems?

We enforce least privilege. Access is strictly role-based and requires documented approval, with quarterly access reviews to prevent unauthorized access.

Is customer data encrypted?

Yes. We use strong encryption for data at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+), ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of customer data.

How does Rhapsody ensure business continuity and disaster recovery?

We maintain a comprehensive Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery plan, tested annually, including data backups, failover procedures, and resilience strategies.

How do you manage third-party and vendor risk?

We have a formal vendor management program that assesses the security posture of sub-processors and key vendors before engagement and on an ongoing basis.

How does Rhapsody ensure compliance with regulations like HIPAA?

Our platform includes encryption, audit logging, and strict access controls to safeguard PHI. We sign BAAs with customers, and our HITRUST certification and independent audits validate these controls.

What is Rhapsody’s approach to data governance?

We provide tools that give customers full control and visibility over their data flows. Customer data is logically isolated, and we only process data according to customer agreements.

How does Rhapsody address GDPR?

We sign DPAs incorporating GDPR Standard Contractual Clauses and rely on mechanisms like the EU-US DPF and UK Extension, applying high standards of data protection to all customers regardless of location.

Does Rhapsody support data residency requirements?

Yes. Our cloud-native services can be deployed in specific regions through partners like AWS and Azure, and customers may self-host. Discuss your specific needs with our team.

Questions about our security or privacy posture?

Our compliance team is here to help. Reach out and we’ll walk you through anything you need.

Legal

Privacy Policy

How Rhapsody handles personal information, including data transferred from the EEA and the United Kingdom under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.

On this page

Overview Data Privacy Framework Scope Definitions Privacy principles Dispute resolution Limitation on principles Contact Communications Privacy Policy Your rights

Last updated July 1, 2026 · Effective date May 1, 2024

Overview

InterOperability Bidco, Inc., dba Rhapsody, provides integration, identity, and terminology software solutions to healthcare providers, health IT companies, insurers, and health information exchanges. We do not directly request personally identifiable information (PII) about individuals (non-employees) for our own behalf or for any purpose of our own.

Rhapsody does not have control over how our customers use the personal information disclosed to them. We provide a safe and secure transfer, storage, and processing mechanism for information gathered by our customers, so it can flow from one application to another. The origin, storage, and transfer of that data is decided by our customers.

Data Privacy Framework

InterOperability Bidco, Inc., dba Rhapsody, complies with the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (EU-US DPF) and the UK Extension to the EU-US DPF, as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce. Rhapsody has certified to the U.S. Department of Commerce that it adheres to the EU-US DPF Principles with regard to the processing of personal data received from the European Union and the United Kingdom in reliance on the EU-US DPF and the UK Extension.

If there is any conflict between the terms in this privacy policy and the EU-US DPF Principles, the Principles govern. To learn more about the Data Privacy Framework program, and to view our certification, visit dataprivacyframework.gov.

Rhapsody is committed to protecting the privacy of individuals in accordance with applicable privacy laws and customer requirements. This policy provides an overarching set of requirements for the management of PII based on internationally accepted privacy principles, forming the foundation of Rhapsody’s global privacy and data protection program. Rhapsody is subject to the investigatory and enforcement powers of the Federal Trade Commission.

Scope

This DPF Privacy Policy applies to all personally identifiable information received by Rhapsody in the United States from the EEA and the United Kingdom, in any format, including electronic, paper, or verbal.

The U.S. entities or subsidiaries of InterOperability Bidco, Inc., dba Rhapsody that also adhere to the EU-US DPF Principles, including as applicable under the UK Extension, and are covered by Rhapsody’s DPF submission, are:

  • Lyniate US Holdings GP, LLC (Delaware)
  • Lyniate New Parent, Inc. (Delaware)
  • InterOperability Holdings, LLC (US)
  • InterOperability Midco, LLC (US)
  • CH Intermediate Holdings, LLC (Delaware)
  • Corepoint Health LLC (Texas)
  • Lyniate US Holdings LP (Delaware)

Definitions

Agent means any third party that collects or uses personal information under the instructions of, and solely for, Rhapsody.

Customer means any customer of Rhapsody, located in the EEA and the United Kingdom, for whom we host or store personal data on our servers in the United States.

Rhapsody means InterOperability Bidco, Inc., dba Rhapsody, its predecessors, successors, subsidiaries, divisions, and groups in the United States.

Personal information means any information or set of information that identifies or could be used by or on behalf of Rhapsody to identify an individual. It does not include information that is encoded, anonymized, or publicly available and not combined with non-public personal information.

Privacy principles

Notice

Rhapsody does not collect personal information directly from individual data subjects in the EEA or the United Kingdom. Where we receive, store, or process personal information from our customers in those regions, we use and disclose it in accordance with the notices provided by our customers, only if consistent with the DPF Principles, and the choices made by the individuals to whom the information relates.

Choice

Rhapsody enables our customers to offer individuals the opportunity to opt out of whether their personal information is disclosed to a third party, or used for a purpose other than the one for which it was originally collected or subsequently authorized. We enable customers to provide individuals with reasonable mechanisms to exercise those choices.

Accountability for onward transfer

Rhapsody does not transfer data to third parties outside of its agents. We obtain assurances from our agents that they will safeguard personal information consistently with this policy, such as a contract obligating the agent to provide at least the same level of protection required by the relevant DPF Principles. Where we know an agent is using or disclosing personal information contrary to this policy, we take reasonable steps to prevent or stop it.

Rhapsody remains responsible and liable under the DPF Principles if a third-party agent it engages processes personal data on its behalf in a manner inconsistent with the Principles, unless Rhapsody proves it is not responsible for the event giving rise to the damage. Rhapsody may be required to disclose personal information in response to a lawful request by public authorities, including to meet national security or law enforcement requirements.

Security

Rhapsody takes reasonable precautions to protect personal information in its possession from loss, misuse, and unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, and destruction, taking into account the risks involved in processing and the nature of the data.

Data integrity and purpose limitation

Rhapsody does not use personal information provided by individuals to our customers; however, we do not control how customers use the information disclosed to them. When directed by a customer to process such information, we use it only in ways compatible with the purposes for which it was collected or subsequently authorized, and take reasonable steps to ensure it is relevant, accurate, complete, and current.

Access and recourse

EU and UK individuals have the right to access their personal information. Upon request, Rhapsody assists our customers in granting individuals access to the personal information it holds about them.

Enforcement and liability

Rhapsody conducts compliance audits of its privacy practices to verify adherence to this policy. Any employee determined to be in violation is subject to disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment.

Dispute resolution

Questions or concerns regarding the use or disclosure of personal information should first be directed to the data controller in question (our customer); or, if the concern is from a customer, to Rhapsody at the address below. Rhapsody will investigate and attempt to resolve complaints by reference to the principles in this policy.

In compliance with the DPF Principles, Rhapsody commits to resolve complaints about your privacy and our collection or use of personal information transferred to the United States under the Data Privacy Frameworks. EU and UK individuals with DPF inquiries should first contact Rhapsody by email at privacy@rhapsody.health.

In compliance with the EU-US DPF and the UK Extension, Rhapsody commits to cooperate and comply with the advice of the panel established by the EU data protection authorities and the UK Information Commissioner’s Office regarding unresolved complaints. If your DPF complaint cannot be resolved through these channels, under certain conditions you may invoke binding arbitration for some residual claims. Rhapsody is subject to the investigatory and enforcement powers of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.

Limitation on application of principles

Adherence by Rhapsody to the DPF Principles may be limited: (a) to the extent required to respond to a legal or ethical obligation; (b) to the extent necessary to meet national security, public interest, or law enforcement obligations; (c) to the extent expressly permitted by an applicable law, rule, or regulation; and (d) to the extent Rhapsody has limited or no control over the actions of its customers regarding use of personal information they have collected.

Rhapsody recognizes the importance of maintaining the privacy of information collected online and maintains a Communications Privacy Policy (below) governing personal information collected through websites it hosts. For personal information transferred from the EEA or the UK to the U.S., the Communications Privacy Policy is subordinate to this policy.

Part two

Communications Privacy Policy

This section applies to Rhapsody’s use of personal information you provide via this website, over the phone, by email, or through any other form of communication, as well as other personal information made available when you visit our website or social media pages. It does not apply to personal information managed by Rhapsody software applications (including clinical records); where we manage that information on our customers’ behalf, we do so under data protection laws and the privacy and security requirements in our customer contracts.

When we refer to “we,” “our,” or “Rhapsody,” we mean our United States company Interoperability Bidco, Inc. and its local subsidiaries in the regions where we operate. Questions about this policy can be sent to Rhapsody’s Chief Privacy Officer at privacy@rhapsody.health.

What information we collect

When you order products or services, make requests, or register to receive materials, we may collect personal information such as your name, company name, address, telephone and fax number, email address, and contact and billing information, depending on what you provide. We also use cookies and collect IP addresses and other information about your device. See our Cookies Policy for more.

How we use your information

Rhapsody may use your personal information for its legitimate business interests, including: responding to your requests; sales and marketing communications about our products, services, newsletters, events, and customer case studies; and website and social media management and improvement. You can opt out of direct marketing emails at any time using the unsubscribe link, or by writing to the Chief Privacy Officer. We may use information in anonymized, aggregated form for marketing and strategic development. We do not sell or trade your information.

Cookies and analytics

We use cookies and third-party analytics services such as Google Analytics to remember your settings, understand how often you visit and what you do on the site, enable sharing to social networks, block abuse, and perform research to improve our website and services. How to reject cookies is explained in our Cookies Policy.

Sharing and international transfer

Generally, Rhapsody will not share your personal information outside our organization. Your information may be processed by third-party suppliers we use, such as digital marketing and analytics providers and cloud-based application providers like Microsoft. Personal information you provide is held in our third-party marketing supplier’s database in the United States, in Rhapsody internal systems in the United States, and/or in cloud applications hosted in other countries, and is accessed by our sales and marketing teams in Boston and other Rhapsody offices for the purposes described here. We maintain adequate privacy and security arrangements through obligations in inter-company and third-party agreements; copies are available on request.

How we protect and retain your information

We use appropriate physical, electronic, and administrative procedures to safeguard the information we collect. We hold personal information only as long as necessary for the purpose you submitted it, and will not keep your contact details longer than three years after our last communication with you.

Your rights

Under applicable laws you have rights to access the personal information we hold about you and have it corrected where necessary, subject to some exceptions. Depending on where you reside, you may also have rights to receive your information in a portable electronic format, to have it erased, to know the third parties it has been shared with, and to object to our processing. You may also lodge a complaint with the relevant data protection authority, and may have rights to compensation. To exercise any of these rights, email the Privacy Officer at privacy@rhapsody.health.

Children

If you are aged 18 or under, please get your parent or guardian’s permission before providing any personal information. Rhapsody does not knowingly solicit, collect, or accept information from or about children via this website. If we become aware that a child has submitted personal information, we delete it as soon as we discover it. If a parent requests review or deletion before we have discovered it, we will honor that request.

Changes to this policy

This policy may be updated from time to time. The date of the most recent revision appears at the top of this page. If you do not agree to a change, please do not continue to submit personal information to Rhapsody.

Questions about your data?

Our privacy team is here to help. Reach out and we’ll walk you through anything you need.

EU-US Data Privacy Framework. InterOperability Bidco, Inc., dba Rhapsody, complies with the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (EU-US DPF) and the UK Extension to the EU-US DPF, as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce. Rhapsody has certified that it adheres to the EU-US DPF Principles with regard to personal data received from the European Union and the United Kingdom in reliance on the EU-US DPF and the UK Extension. If there is any conflict between our privacy policy and the DPF Principles, the Principles govern. To learn more and view our certification, visit dataprivacyframework.gov.
